615.text: H0629 shows a far wider occurrence spread (7 verses) and a broader register than H0149's single occurrence: H0629 covers financial payment (6.8), the royal decree formula 'with all diligence' (6.12, 7.21), ongoing building progress (5.8), judicial severity/'strictly' (7.26), and cultic purchase/offering (7.17), whereas H0149's lone attestation (7.23) sits specifically in the preventive-of-wrath register tied to temple provisioning -- H0629 is the general-purpose administrative-thoroughness adverb of the corpus while H0149 appears as a narrower, single-context reinforcement of the same idea.

617.text: Morphologically, both H0149 and H0629 are invariant adverbs (AD) across every occurrence in this subgroup -- there is no stem/voice variation to check for meaning-relevance in either term; both are fixed adverbial intensifiers with no active/passive/causative distinction possible, a genuine no-distinction-found result for the morph-reading requirement.

828.text: The immediate response denoted (complete, prompt execution of a command) is consistent across every occurrence of both strongs -- payment 'in full without delay' (6.8), decree carried out 'with all diligence' (6.12, 7.21, 6.13), building progressing 'diligently' (5.8), purchase/offering 'with all diligence' (7.17), judgment executed 'strictly' (7.26), and compliance 'in full' (7.23) all show the same uniform thoroughness-response, varying only in the domain of the act, not in the quality of response.

830.text: No transformation of a person is in view at all -- the terms qualify the manner of a discrete administrative act, not a change of state in the agent, so reversibility/irreversibility does not apply.

841.text: It crosses covenantal boundaries -- H0629/H0149 appear in decrees issued by pagan Persian kings (Darius, Artaxerxes) enforcing compliance both for civil/administrative matters (payment, building) and for the covenant people's temple worship (offerings, judgment under 'the law of your God'), showing the diligence-formula is a shared administrative idiom usable by non-covenant authority even when the object of compliance is covenantal (temple provisioning).

844.text: Where the characteristic moves toward God (Ezra.7.17, buying and offering sacrifices 'with all diligence' at the altar of God's house; Ezra.7.23, complying 'in full' with what God has decreed to avoid his wrath), the inner posture required is submissive exactness before divine authority -- treating God's decree with the same unhesitating completeness demanded of a royal command, differing only in that the consequence invoked is divine wrath rather than royal penalty.

845.text: The human-to-God direction (7.17, 7.23) shows a relationship of subordination under decree -- the person relates to God as a subject relates to a sovereign, owing exact and complete compliance to avoid wrath, a relationship framed in legal/administrative terms rather than intimate or covenantal-love terms.

863.text: Simple in structure -- both H0629 and H0149 are single unanalyzed adverbs with no compound constituent elements; they intensify a verb directly without combining separate inner-being components.

876.text: The distinction between H0629 and H0149 is one of degree/frequency and rhetorical emphasis, not kind, direction, or constitutional level -- both terms occupy the identical semantic and grammatical niche (adverb of manner intensifying compliance-verbs), differing only in how widely attested and how gravely-framed each occurrence is.

2972.text: Across its full occurrence list H8426 clusters into three recurring realizations of one lexeme: (1) the concrete thank-offering sacrifice (Lev.7.12 x2, Lev.7.13, Lev.7.15, Lev.22.29, Ps.50.14, Ps.50.23, Ps.107.22, Ps.116.17, Amos.4.5, Jonah.2.9, 2Chr.29.31 x2, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11), (2) the vocal/manner accompaniment of praise, 'with/in thanksgiving' (Ps.69.30, Ps.26.7, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Isa.51.3), and (3) the institutional thanksgiving choir/procession/company (Neh.12.27, Neh.12.31, Neh.12.38, Neh.12.40, Ps.42.4). A fourth, rarer sense realizes it as verbal confession (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11). This is a single strong showing internally the full sense-range attributed to the subgroup label (hymn, choir, offering) without needing a second member strong to supply any of these senses.

2973.text: Since H8426 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, there is no second lexeme to compare it against directly; the meaningful cross-comparison available is internal -- between H8426's own sacrificial/cultic-object occurrences (e.g. Lev.7.12-15, Lev.22.29, 2Chr.29.31, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11, Amos.4.5) versus its choir/procession-as-institution occurrences (Neh.12.27-40, Ps.42.4) versus its purely adverbial/manner occurrences ('with thanksgiving', e.g. Ps.69.30, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Ps.26.7). These three groupings do not overlap grammatically: the sacrificial sense is always the head noun or a construct-genitive qualifier of an offering-word (zebach, shelamim), the choir sense functions as a collective-body noun (subject or object of appointment/movement verbs), and the manner sense is marked by a preposition (b-) modifying a separate main verb of praise. No morphological distinction (all occurrences are the same feminine noun stem, singular or plural absolute/construct) drives this three-way split -- it is purely syntactic/contextual, meaning the noun's referent is disambiguated entirely by its syntactic role in each verse rather than by any inflectional change.

2976.text: Because this subgroup contains only one member strong (H8426), there is no other subgroup-member strong against which to run a genuine cross-strong tightly-related/no-direct-connection comparison; the subgroup's 'own core task' of synergising member strongs against each other therefore has no second party within E_todah_offering_noun itself -- the meaningful comparison work is instead the internal sense-range analysis captured in the other observations here, and any cross-strong work against sibling cluster strongs (e.g. H3034) belongs to a different subgroup/cluster-level pass, not this one.

3142.text: Both patterns occur: in Ps.50.23 and Ps.116.17 thanksgiving follows recognition of benefit/salvation already received (a belief precedes the act), while in Josh.7.19 the call to give todah (confession) precedes and is meant to produce a changed belief/admission in Achan -- the offering can express a settled conviction or be the means of producing one.

3146.text: As a repeatable liturgical/sacrificial act (offered again and again -- Lev.7.12-15, 22.29, Ps.50.14 'perform your vows'), todah does not describe a one-time irreversible transformation but a recurring, renewable practice; no verse depicts it as a permanent, one-way change of state.

3147.text: The mechanism differs sharply by context: in the cultic-legal texts (Leviticus) it operates through prescribed sacrificial procedure (bread, oil, timing of eating); in the Psalms it operates through vocal/musical praise (song, instruments, joyful noise); in Nehemiah it operates through organized communal procession/choir; and in Joshua/Ezra it operates through spoken confession -- the same noun realized through markedly different concrete mechanisms.

3148.text: Todah's role as a fitting, God-desired response to divine goodness (Ps.50.14,23; Ps.100.4) reads as belonging to created design -- the proper creaturely posture toward the Creator -- while its confessional realization (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11), required because of sin, reads as belonging to the fallen condition; the single lexeme thus spans both.

3151.text: The mode of operation varies by context: as a sacrificial-cultic act performed at the altar (Lev.7.12-15, 22.29), as a vocal/musical act in corporate worship (Ps.95.2, 100.4, 147.7), as an institutional choir/procession (Neh.12.27-40), and as spoken confession under confrontation (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11) -- direction is consistently human-to-God except in the confession cases which are human-to-human-under-divine-authority (Achan to Joshua/the Lord).

3154.text: Amos.4.5 depicts todah offered ironically/emptily ('for so you love to do' amid rebuke), showing the characteristic blocked or distorted when performed as hollow ritual detached from covenant faithfulness -- external form without genuine acknowledgment. No angelic/adversarial interference is shown in any occurrence.

3155.text: Amos.4.5 implies a person performing todah without it 'taking hold' rightly (empty ritual), but the inner-being state of such a person (their disposition toward God underneath the ritual) is not directly described in this verse; resolving it needs the surrounding oracle in Amos 4 describing Israel's actual heart-condition.

3157.text: In every occurrence todah operates strictly within the covenantal context of Israel's relationship with the Lord (temple, altar, corporate worship); the evidence shows no instance of it crossing covenantal boundaries to non-covenant nations or peoples.

3158.text: The relational scope of todah includes the covenant worshipper (individual or corporate/Israel), directed toward the Lord as recipient; included also are the priests and Levites who administer or lead it (Neh.12.27-40). Excluded from the evidence are foreign nations, non-covenant peoples, and any depiction of todah offered to or received from any being other than the Lord.

3159.text: Todah's consistent presence in worship contexts and its designed place as the response God desires (Ps.50.14,23) over mere ritual sacrifice suggests thanksgiving belongs to the proper functioning of the divine image in the human person -- a capacity for grateful acknowledgment that reflects rightly-ordered relationship with the Creator; its absence or hollow performance (Amos.4.5) signals a marred expression of that same capacity.

3163.text: Todah is an exclusively creaturely analogue rather than a shared characteristic with God -- it is the creature's response to the Creator (never God giving thanks to a human), so no occurrence shows it as a shared attribute; it exists only on the human side of the relationship.

3164.text: Where todah is genuinely present and rightly ordered (Ps.50.23, 2Chr.29.31), it indicates a functioning, rightly-oriented divine image responsive to God; where it is offered as hollow ritual (Amos.4.5) or required because of covenant breach (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11), it indicates the image is present but marred or in need of restoration through confession.

3165.text: Todah engages the vocal/speech level (song, proclamation, confession -- Ps.26.7, Ps.147.7, Josh.7.19) and the bodily/ritual-action level (sacrifice offered, loaves brought -- Lev.7.12-15) but the evidence never depicts it engaging a purely internal/unspoken level in isolation -- it is always externalized, either in speech or material offering, showing its seat is fundamentally expressive rather than private. Where a body link exists (the sacrificial act), it is functional -- the body/materials serve as the vehicle carrying the inner acknowledgment into concrete cultic form.

3166.text: Where a body link exists, it runs from inner disposition/soul outward through the body (bringing an offering, singing, speaking) -- soul/spirit expressing through bodily/material act; there is no evidence of the reverse direction (the body/ritual feeding back to shape the soul) within these occurrences themselves.

3167.text: Todah moves outward from the human person toward God (never onto the person from an external spirit); its sequence runs from an inward recognition of divine benefit to an outward act of speech or offering directed to God -- a soul-to-expression movement, with no instance of external spiritual origination.

3169.text: God's desire for and acceptance of todah as the true sacrifice he wants (Ps.50.14,23) shows his disposition to value relational, grateful acknowledgment over mere ritual performance -- he desires genuine covenant communion, not empty formality.

3174.text: No occurrence of H8426 shows adversarial spiritual activity interfering with or targeting thanksgiving; the only distortion evidenced is the human hollowing-out of ritual into empty performance (Amos.4.5), not an external adversarial agent's action.

3176.text: The origin is consistently single -- the human worshipper (individual or corporate) as the one who offers, sings, or confesses todah toward God -- across every context (legal-cultic, psalmic, prophetic, historical); it does not change to a different originating source in any occurrence.

3178.text: Todah is best characterized as an act/offering (a concrete, performable/presentable thing -- a song sung, a sacrifice brought, a confession spoken) rather than a settled disposition or abstract quality; its noun-form crystallizes an act into a nameable liturgical entity.

3179.text: Todah is compound: it combines an inner disposition of grateful/confessing acknowledgment with an outward, often material or vocal, form of expression (offering, song, procession) -- the two elements (disposition and enacted form) are inseparable in the term's usage.

3180.text: The structural opposite of todah is hollow, self-serving ritual performed without genuine acknowledgment (as rebuked in Amos.4.5) or, more fundamentally, silence/withholding of acknowledgment in the face of benefit received or wrongdoing committed -- an unacknowledging heart that neither confesses nor gives thanks.

14181.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: Kin offence hardens. "A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city, and quarreling is like the bars of a castle" (Pro 18:19). The closer the tie, the harder the wall. This is the reverse of Gen 13's reason for yielding ("for we are kinsmen"); Brothers' anger takes the form of imposed labour: "My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!" (Song 1:6). The anger is felt by the one it lands on as the loss of her own vineyard. The next verse turns straight to "you whom my soul loves" (1:7); Edom against his brother: anger that never turns away. Edom "pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath forever" (Amo 1:11). God will deal with Edom "according to the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them" (Eze 35:11), with its speech: "They are given us to devour" (35:12); This is exactly the opposite of Gen 27:44–45. There Rebekah waits for Esau's anger to "turn away" and for him to "forget", and it does (Gen 33:4). Esau the man let his anger pass. Edom, his nation, "kept his wrath forever". The same bloodline shows anger's two courses; Amo 1:9 names the same failure for Tyre: "did not remember the covenant of brotherhood"; Anger at a brother judged like murder, and the remedy is reconciliation before worship: "everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment" (Mat 5:22); "leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother" (5:24). The worship waits on the relationship; Brothers in the work part without the yielding: "there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark … but Paul chose Silas" (Act 15:39–40). It began over Mark, "who had withdrawn from them" (15:38). Separation, as in Gen 13:11, but here neither party gives the other the choice. Both are "commended … to the grace of the Lord" (15:40) and the work goes on in two directions; Seat : none in-verse or ±2. The next verse after Song 1:6 has "you whom my soul loves" (Song 1:7). Genuine. The bearer's own. The one who bears her brothers' anger turns at once to the one her soul loves.

16085.text: What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" (5); "Saul listened … Saul swore, 'As the Lord lives, he shall not be put to death'" (6); War again; David's victory (8); "a harmful spirit from the Lord came upon Saul" (9) [O]

16094.text: Revisit (delta) — the law also refuses a price, and it says where (context Num 35:30–34): "you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death" (31); "you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge" (32); "no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it" (33); "Whoever takes a human life shall surely be put to death" (Lev 24:17); [Claude reading] The line falls at bloodshed. Exo 30 and Pro 13:8 price a life. Num 35 refuses a price for the life that took a life. Only that life answers for the blood. Which side of the line a killer stands on is settled by his heart toward the dead man (§16.6).; Where the law refuses, two other voices name a ransom: Elihu's mediator: "Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom" (Job 33:24; §16.4); Love: "If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised" (Song 8:7; §16.3). Love has no price, as the soul has none in Mat 16:26.

16211.text: 16.10 Life risked "to death" for others — the OT precedent: "Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death" (Judg 5:18). This is in the same song as "March on, my soul, with might!" (5:21; §3.2).; "Our life for yours even to death!" (Jos 2:14; §4 revisit); David "took his life in his hand" against the Philistine (1Sa 19:5); The men to David: "If half of us die, they will not care [*set heart*] about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us" (2Sa 18:3). The enemy's heart is indifferent to many deaths. One life is weighed at ten thousand.; "the men who were seeking your life are dead" (Exo 4:19) → Moses returns (4:20). 16726.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Moral condition is predicated above all of the heart. The heart is: upright, whole, pure, clean or blameless (§1); evil, crooked, perverse, twisted, false or double (§2, §4, §5); proud / high or humbled / tender (§9, §10); It is also where sin is stored, engraved or hidden (§3.3). God tests and weighs it (Psa 7:9; Pro 21:2; Luk 16:15; Act 15:8). The heart is the organ that is morally evaluated.; The soul (*nephesh*) is the accountable person and the life at stake.; It sins, realises guilt, bears iniquity and is cut off (§3.1). It is the unfaithful party (§5).; It is the life that righteousness delivers (§1.7) and that sin injures (§3.2).; It is the innocent blood that is shed (§1.7). It is afflicted on holy days (§7.5).; At the limit it is the corpse that defiles (§8.2).; The soul is less often *evaluated* (righteous soul: 2Pe 2:8; puffed-up soul: Hab 2:4) than *answerable*.; The human spirit is evaluated chiefly on the pride–humility axis (§9.2, §10.2): haughty, proud, hardened, lowly, poor, contrite. Otherwise it is: without deceit (Psa 32:2); right / clean (Psa 51:10); faithful in marriage (Mal 2:15–16); trustworthy (Pro 11:13); holy or defiled with the body (1Co 7:34; 2Co 7:1); sanctified with soul and body (1Th 5:23); perfected in the righteous dead (Heb 12:23); weighed (Pro 16:2); broken by a perverse tongue (Pro 15:4); [observation, not a count]; Other spirits carry the negative moral adjectives. They are evil / harmful (§2.1, 15 verses), unclean (§8.1, 23 verses) and lying / deceitful (§4.1, 6 verses). They are the moral clusters' names turned into kinds of spirit.; In the OT some are sent by God (1Sa 16; Judg 9:23; 1Ki 22:22–23).; In the NT they indwell and are cast out.; The Holy Spirit is the positive counterpart, and the one against whom human sin is directed: blasphemed, lied to, grieved, resisted, outraged (§2.4, §4.2, §7.1).; Inner vs outer purity.; Ritual clean / unclean / holy vocabulary attaches to flesh, body and *nephesh*-as-person or corpse.; Moral purity attaches to heart, spirit, soul and conscience.; Several texts deliberately contrast the two: Psa 24:4; 2Ch 30:19; Mar 7:19–21; Heb 9:13–14; 10:22; Jam 4:8.

16727.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Conscience is the NT's named moral-awareness faculty. It can be clear, pure, good, evil, defiled, seared, weak or wounded. It testifies (2Co 1:12; Rom 9:1) and is purified by Christ's blood (Heb 9:14). It is frequently paired with the heart (1Ti 1:5; Heb 10:22).; The OT does this work with the heart: "David's heart struck him" (2Sa 24:10); "my heart does not reproach me" (Job 27:6).; The Levitical "realizes his guilt" (Lev 5) describes the same moment without naming an organ.; The heart deceives itself and is the source of evil.; It deceives its owner: Jer 17:9; Obd 3; Isa 44:20.; Evil comes from it: Gen 6:5; Mat 15:19; Luk 6:45.; Its evil hides behind speech: Psa 28:3; 41:6; Pro 26:23–25.; Pride deceives the heart that holds it (Obd 3), linking M08 and M14.; Flesh carries on from Batch C (§11.5).; OT: flesh is the ritual body and meat — clean or unclean, holy or tainted.; NT Pauline: flesh is the seat of sin (Rom 7–8; Gal 5:19) and the ground of false boasting (Phili 3:3).; Positive NT uses remain: "holy … in his body of flesh" (Col 1:22); "bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).; Wind and breath are the image of moral emptiness: iniquity takes us away like wind (Isa 64:6); the wicked are chaff (Psa 1:4); "wind and lies" (Mic 2:11); idols with no breath (Jer 10:14); the *hevel* + *rûaḥ* refrain (Ecc); Only the messianic "breath of his lips" (Isa 11:4) and the breath that conveys the Holy Spirit (Joh 20:22) are active and effective.; Fringe worth keeping: *nephesh* = corpse as the defiling body (§8.2); the "high heart" that is pride or courage depending on direction (2Ch 17:6 vs 2Ch 32:25); the heart that strikes or does not reproach — pre-conscience (§3.3, §9.5); sin against one's own soul (§3.2); the servant's soul as guilt offering (§3.6); lies that kill and keep alive souls (Eze 13:19); the spirit of jealousy that comes whether or not the defilement is real (Num 5:14); false humility of the flesh (Col 2:18, 23); the thorn in the flesh against conceit (2Co 12:7); Eliab misreading David's heart (1Sa 17:28); "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" (2Ki 10:15)

(Jos 2:14); David "took his life in his hand" (1Sa 19:5); Rev 12:11 ("loved not their lives even unto death") uses the same shape. What the NT adds is the object ("for the name of the Lord Jesus", Act 21:13) and the example ("poured out his soul to death", Isa 53:12).

16932.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The merry heart is a threshold state. In every narrative it comes after eating and drinking and immediately before a decisive event, which others usually initiate. The good heart lowers guard. What enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder (Amnon); exposure and anger (Vashti, Ahasuerus); mockery turned to catastrophe (Samson); outrage (Gibeah); approach and redemption (Ruth); a dead heart the next morning (Nabal); God's claim on the soul (the rich fool); The heart's condition swings overnight. Nabal: merry heart → dead heart (1Sa 25:36–37). Ahasuerus: merry heart → burning anger (Est 1:10–12). The heart's state is not stable; wine sets it high, and news or refusal drops it.; 1Ki 21 joins spirit and heart. Ahab's spirit is vexed and he stops eating. Jezebel prescribes food and a good heart, secured by injustice. A spirit-state is "cured" by manufacturing a heart-state — the only place in the batch where one is treated through the other.; Positive merriment exists outside the narratives: "they … went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1Ki 8:66); "A joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "let your heart cheer you … But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9); When the heart is good because of God, no threshold event follows. When it is good from wine, one does.; Revisit (Batch G) — the threshold pattern extended: The step before the merry heart: "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5, 8). The father-in-law alternates *strengthen* (5, 8) and *merry* (6, 9). Each round delays departure (G §3.1).; The threshold engineered and refused: David "made him drunk" (2Sa 11:13). Uriah, who had sworn "as your soul lives, I will not do this thing" (11:11), still does not go home. The next morning: the death letter (11:14–15) (G §4).; The soul's version: "prepare for me delicious food … that my soul may bless you" (Gen 27:4). 19222.text: Seat.; In the verse: 2Sa 18:13 "if I had dealt treacherously against his life". *Nephesh* here is Absalom's life, the other party's, in its life sense. It is the life that would have been taken, not an inner faculty. New in v3: the inner movement of the verse (restraint by knowing one will be seen) belongs to the soldier, and it has no seat word. This verse was not read in the M47 batches.; In the passage, the bearer's own (genuine): Psa 38:9 stands between "the tumult of my heart" (38:8) and "My heart throbs; my strength fails me" (38:10). The sighing that is not hidden from God is a heart's sighing. Exposure here is received as comfort, because what is seen is the heart's pain.; In the passage, the offender's (genuine): Isa 29:15, "you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel", follows 29:13, "their hearts are far from me". The attempt to hide counsel comes from a heart already far off. This is the same heart that §8 (Isa 29:14) reads as losing its discernment. Batch G v3 §12.3 ("Honour with lips, heart far") read 29:13 itself.; New in v3, within one psalm: Psa 139 holds §6 and §11 together. "My frame was not hidden from you" (139:15, EX) and "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts [anxious thoughts]" (139:23, AX; Batch A v3 §6 "God searching the anxious heart"). Being wholly seen, accepted as a fact at 139:15, becomes a search the psalmist asks for at 139:23. The seat named in the request is the heart, and the anxieties in it. The verse before 139:15 gives the knowing from the human side: "I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well" (139:14). God sees the frame (139:15), and the soul knows it has been made (139:14). Two knowings meet: God's knowledge of the person, and the soul's knowledge of being known and made. Exposure here produces praise.

19678.text: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him": The law concerns *"a slave who has escaped from his master to you"*. Israel is told *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15). Then the choice is handed to the slave: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (v16).; The man who escaped had no say over where he lived. The law gives it back to him. The choice is his, and its ground is his own good: *"wherever it suits him"* is literally "in what is good to him" (H2896A). Israel's part is to honour it: not to hand him back, and not to *"wrong him"* (H3238, to oppress).; The phrase is a weighty one in Deuteronomy. *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same shape as the phrase Deuteronomy uses for the Lord’s own choosing: *"the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes"* (12:5); *"the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes"* (12:14). The words (place, that, choose, in one of your …) are the same (H4725, H0977). I read this as the law giving the escaped slave, in his own small measure, the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw the comparison.

19835.text: H0977, "choose". This is the ordinary verb, and it carries most of these verses. The ESV renders it in several ways: *"choose"*; *"desire"*: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38); *"to be chosen"* in the sense of preferred: *"To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16); The same verb is used of the Lord choosing the place for his name (Deu 12:5, 14), and of the Lord's answering choice: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (Isa 66:4).

19858.text: A choice that is honoured: Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).; The phrase *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same wording as *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deu 12:5, 14). I read this as the law giving the slave a small share of the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw this comparison (open item).

20271.text: The held phrasing in 10.7. The working note in 10.7 holds the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 (*"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"*) and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14. Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*.
